source.title: Cliff-Learning
source.authors: T. T. Wang; Igor Zablotchi; Nir Shavit; Jonathan S. Rosenfeld

record.tranche_reason: The study measures downstream data-scaling and argues that a single power law needs qualification: transfer-learning curves can show a transient faster-than-power-law cliff at low data, then return to power-law behavior at large data.
record.gate_note: The study tests data-scaling of transfer learning and toy learning problems, not language-model held-out pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute scaling. Results cited from other studies, including data-pruning curves, are not recorded as the study's own results. Exact plotted values are not transcribed in the text, so relevant plot results are recorded as figure only.
record.test_reason: The study measures how image-classification transfer error scales with downstream data for CLIP and BeIT models. This is the fine-tuning/transfer regime named in V5. It argues that the power-law form fails at low n: there is a faster-than-power-law 'cliff' before the curves revert to power laws at large n. It does not test language-model pretraining loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Broadly correct. The authors conclude that low-data transfer learning often shows cliff-learning (faster-than-power-law gains), whose strength reflects how well the learned prior fits the task. Cliffs are transient: at large n, models of different quality scale as power laws with similar exponents but different A and E. Hernandez et al. missed cliffs because they worked only in the large-n regime.
record.recipe_differences: The study measures downstream test error as a function of downstream training data, rather than held-out language-model pretraining loss as a function of parameters, tokens, or compute.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome differs by dataset (CIFAR-10 versus SVHN), foundation-model quality, and transfer method (linear probe, full fine-tuning, k-NN probe, and fully connected probe); regularization also changes the toy-network curve.

fits_no_version.finding: Toy estimators show sharp or soft cliffs at a critical sample count when the algorithm's prior matches the task (least squares, regularized MLP, Gaussian classifier). Without that match they show power-law scaling.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Prior–task compatibility determines whether data scaling departs from a power law (cliff-learning).

record.problems: The study does not test language-model pretraining loss or parameter/token/compute scaling. Many relevant curve values are reported only in figures. Some comparisons use curves extracted from cited papers rather than experiments run by these authors.
record.rows_left_out: No rows omitted for the 60-row limit.

Dependence of language-model exponents or compute-optimal split on parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method.
All of V6. The study varies downstream sample count, not model scale or pretraining loss.

record.verdict_notes: Short workshop-style preprint. Every curve value is figure only and no exponents are fitted, so V5 and V7 verdicts rest on the authors' qualitative descriptions. From-scratch and data-pruning baselines are digitized from cited papers (Rosenfeld 2019, Bahri 2021, Sorscher 2022b), not rerun. Model sizes are not stated beyond CLIP variant names.

Prediction of much larger language-model runs from fits to small runs.
Architecture-shape effects at fixed parameter count.

rows.subject: Fully connected ReLU network, 3 hidden layers
rows.stage_stated: trained with Adam on a 2D harmonic-function task
rows.operation_detail: Measured validation-MSE scaling with number of training examples, with and without bandwidth regularization.
rows.measure: Validation MSE; without regularization curves follow a power-law trend and plateau at a level governed by network size; with bandwidth regularization there is a soft cliff near n=(2B+1)².
rows.value: Unregularized: power-law trend and plateau. Regularized: soft cliff near n=(2B+1)².
rows.note: The authors note slightly non-monotonic scaling after the initial regularized cliff.
rows.check: Small MLP on a synthetic 2D harmonic regression task. Bandwidth regularization is an intervention built to produce the cliff. Not a V5 modality or training regime.
